1-2: Even and odd numbers: which number of a list is even.
Beads in a repeating pattern of two colours: the colour of a given bead.
Children in pairs: how many are left without a pair.
A lamp or a door switched again and again: on or off, open or shut, after a given number of turns.
Odd or even numbers in order, such as the house numbers on one side of a street: a given one, or how many up to a number.
A sum of a few odd numbers: even or odd, by how many numbers there are.
A circle of boys and girls standing in turn: how many of each.
A frog jumping two stones at a time: which stones it can land on.
Sweets shared equally between two friends and between some other number of friends.
Coins turned over one at a time: after how many turns they can all lie the other way up.
A number added to itself, or anything made of two equal halves, such as a double domino: the total is always even.
Two children taking turns, the first on every odd turn: whose turn a given one is, such as the ninth.
A strip of squares filled with dominoes, two squares each: a strip of an odd number of squares always leaves one empty.
Two numbers next to each other in counting, such as 7 and 8: one is even and the other odd, so their sum is odd.
3-4: The sum of two numbers is odd: what the other number can be.
A number of things split into two groups: the groups can differ by an even number only when the whole is even, and by an odd number only when it is odd.
Plus and minus signs put between numbers in a row: whichever signs are chosen, the result is even or odd just as the plain sum is.
A product of two numbers is odd: what that says about both of them.
Sheets torn out of a book: each holds an odd page and the next even one, so the two numbers on a sheet add up to an odd number.
A sum written in a column with its digits marked only even or odd: the evenness of each column, with what is carried, tells which digits can stand there.
The sum of the odd numbers against the sum of the even numbers in a range.
Points or children in a row with a new one put between every two neighbours: the count becomes odd, however many there were.
A sheet torn up again and again, one piece at a time into three parts or five: every tear adds an even number of pieces, so their count stays odd.
Number cards split into two piles with equal sums: which sets can be split.
Gears in a ring, each turning the next one the other way: with an odd number of gears none of them can turn.
Fruits picked by rules that change the number of one kind by two or not at all: that number stays even or odd, which tells the last fruit.
Creatures with three hands each, holding hands so that no hand is free: an odd number of them cannot do it.
5-6: Steps that add or multiply: which numbers can be reached.
A knight on a chessboard: the colour of its square after some moves.
A sum of many numbers is odd: how many of them can be even.
Adding 1 to two numbers at a time: the fewest steps to make them all equal.
Dominoes on a board with two corners cut off: how many fit.
A walk on a grid of squares: whether it can end where it began after an odd number of steps.
Frogs jumping over one another on a line: which places are possible.
Switching three lamps in a row at a time: whether all of them can be on.
Bugs crawling to neighbouring squares: how many squares can be left empty.
Handshakes at a party: how many people shook an odd number of hands.
Stories of different lengths in a book, each starting on a new page: a story of an odd length moves the next start from an odd page to an even one or back.
People standing so that all their distances differ, each shooting the nearest one: with an odd number of them, someone stays dry.
Coins of three colours, two of different colours traded for one of the third: whether each difference between the counts is even never changes.
A jumper on numbered points round a circle whose step depends on whether its point is odd or even: its places soon repeat in a cycle.
The squares of a chessboard numbered row by row: a row has an even number of squares, so the odd numbers lie on one colour in a row and on the other in the next.
Children round a table where each child and both neighbours together hold an odd number of sweets: the numbers repeat every three places, so unless three divides the count, each holds an odd number.
A number written as a sum of odd numbers in a row: an odd count of them gives an odd sum, and an even count a multiple of four.
Numbers chosen from a small set and told only by their product: when that product cannot tell whether their sum is odd or even.
